chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Is an Inflation Regime?

lessons.title: How Economists and Central Banks Read a Regime Shift: CPI, WPI, and Core Inflation

children.text: You now know what a regime is and which of the three engines drives it. The harder, more useful skill is spotting a regime shift while it is still forming, not three months later once the CPI prints have already confirmed it. By the time a shift is obvious in the headline number, the RBI has usually already started reacting and bond and gold prices have already moved. Central banks and serious analysts do not wait for the CPI alone; they read a wider toolkit of leading indicators alongside it.

body.text: By the time a regime shift shows up clearly across three straight CPI prints, the market has usually already repriced it. The real edge is in reading the leading indicators before the confirmation arrives.

The RBI does not just react to the last CPI print. Its bi-monthly Monetary Policy Report publishes its own forward inflation forecast. When the market's own read of where inflation is heading diverges sharply from the RBI's stated forecast, that gap is itself a signal worth watching.

children.text: Headline CPI is a year-on-year number: this month's price level compared with the same month a year ago. That creates a distortion analysts call the

. If petrol prices spiked sharply in a given month last year and have stayed flat since, this year's year-on-year comparison will show inflation falling, even though nothing has actually gotten cheaper on the ground. The reverse also happens: a low base a year ago can make a perfectly normal price rise look like a dangerous spike. Reading a single YoY print without checking what the base looked like twelve months back is one of the most common mistakes retail investors make when they panic-sell on a scary-looking inflation headline.

body.caption: The CPI print you see every month is this ratio. The denominator, last year's price level, is doing as much work as this year's actual price move.

body.title: Name the Distortion
body.textWithBlank: When an unusually high or low price level from twelve months ago drops out of the year-on-year comparison window and distorts the current inflation print without any real change in prices today, this is called the ___.
body.explanation: The base effect is not a new inflation engine, it is a measurement artifact of comparing against last year's base. Always check what the base looked like before reacting to a sharp YoY swing.

children.text: CPI is a lagging confirmation, not an early warning. Four indicators tend to move first. The PMI (Purchasing Managers' Index) surveys, released in the first few days of the following month, well before the CPI print, ask factory and services purchasing managers directly whether input and output prices are rising, giving a read on cost pressure before it shows up at the retail level. The RBI's own Inflation Expectations Survey of Households, published alongside its Monetary Policy Report, captures what ordinary households expect prices to do over the next few months and the next year, and expectations that drift up tend to become self-fulfilling through wage demands. The gap between WPI and CPI, the

, flags cost pressure sitting at the wholesale or factory-gate level that has not yet been passed through to what households pay. And the USD/INR exchange rate, tracked live on NSE currency derivatives, matters directly because a weaker rupee raises the landed cost of everything India imports, oil and edible oil most of all.

body.caption: Where to look before the CPI print confirms a shift

cells: Cost pressure building in factories and services, ahead of retail pass-through
Monthly Manufacturing and Services PMI releases
What households expect prices to do next; feeds directly into MPC deliberations
Pipeline cost pressure at the wholesale level not yet passed to retail
Monthly WPI and CPI releases from MOSPI and the Commerce Ministry
Imported inflation risk through the exchange rate and fuel costs
NSE currency derivatives, MCX crude and Brent benchmarks

body.label: Release Order Matters
body.context: PMI surveys land in the first few days of the month, CPI follows roughly a week or two later, and quarterly GDP data arrives with the longest lag of all. If you are only watching CPI, you are already reading old news.

children.text: Putting It Together: A Regime-Shift Checklist

body.title: Before You Call a Regime Shift, Check
steps: Is core CPI (ex food and fuel) trending up for two or more consecutive quarters, not just one noisy headline print?
Are PMI input prices rising faster than PMI output prices, meaning businesses are absorbing cost pressure they have not yet passed on?
Has the rupee depreciated meaningfully against the dollar in the last one to two months?
Are household inflation expectations in the RBI's survey climbing, not just holding steady?
Is the move visible across two or more independent indicators, not just one metric moving on its own?

body.title: Signal or Noise?
body.scenario: PMI input prices have risen for three straight months. Core CPI has drifted up from 4.1% to 4.8% over two quarters. The rupee has weakened about 4% against the dollar in sixty days. Headline CPI, however, is still comfortably inside the RBI's tolerance band at 5.1%.
body.prompt: Is this the early stage of a genuine regime shift, or is it noise you should ignore until the headline CPI print itself moves? Use the checklist above to justify your answer.
body.modelAnswer: This reads as an early, genuine shift rather than noise, precisely because it satisfies the checklist: the move shows up across core CPI, PMI input prices, and the currency together, not in a single volatile metric. Headline CPI staying inside the comfort band does not mean the shift is not happening, it means the shift has not yet fully worked through to the number everyone else is watching. An analyst who waits for headline CPI to confirm it will be reacting roughly a quarter behind an analyst who read the leading indicators converging.

points: CPI confirms a regime shift; it rarely predicts one. PMI, household inflation expectations, the WPI-CPI wedge, and USD/INR tend to move first.
The base effect can make a stable inflation environment look like it is falling, or a normal rise look like a spike, purely because of what happened to prices twelve months ago.
The RBI publishes its own forward inflation forecast in its Monetary Policy Report; a wide gap between that forecast and the market's own read is itself information.
One indicator moving is noise. Two or more independent indicators, core CPI, PMI input prices, the currency, and inflation expectations, moving together is a real signal.
This checklist is the toolkit you will apply for the rest of the course, starting with the global classics in the next chapter.
